tldr: We introduce DWMP (Dual World Model Policy), which linearizes highly nonlinear proprioception using Koopman operators and compresses high-dimensional depth images using a recurrent state-space model. In simulation, it achieves an obstacle traversal success rate roughly 10% higher than distillation baselines, and it successfully traverses randomized obstacle layouts on a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
hero_caption: Overall training pipeline of the proposed DWMP framework. In Phase 1, dual world models are pre-trained using exploration data collected from a teacher policy with privileged environment information. In Phase 2, a student policy using only onboard sensors receives latent representations from the world models to generate actions, while fine-tuning the encoders to adapt to the student's own data distribution.
overview:
For a humanoid robot to navigate cluttered obstacle fields toward a goal, it must skillfully combine proprioception—which captures body posture and joint motions—with vision (depth images) that captures the geometry of the scene ahead. However, conventional multimodal reinforcement learning and teacher-student distillation frameworks often simply concatenate these two sensor streams or pass them through non-predictive feature extractors. As a result, the student policy ends up acting as a purely reactive imitator, unable to anticipate how the environment and its own dynamics will evolve over time.

To address this, the authors focus on the fundamentally different characteristics of the two modalities. Proprioceptive observations are low-dimensional but exhibit extreme nonlinearity driven by complex contact and joint dynamics. In contrast, egocentric depth images are high-dimensional, noisy, and highly redundant. Instead of ignoring these differences and blending them into a single monolithic model, the authors designed DWMP (Dual World Model Policy), which equips the robot with two specialized, parallel world models.

Specifically, an Auto-Koopman network based on Koopman operator theory is applied to proprioceptive dynamics. It lifts the nonlinear system into a high-dimensional latent space where its temporal evolution is approximately linear. For vision, a recurrent state-space model (RSSM)—widely known from Dreamer—is used to compress depth images spatio-temporally into compact stochastic states. By concatenating these two latent states and feeding them into the student actor policy, the robot can leverage both linearized, easy-to-predict dynamics features and compact visual features that retain obstacle geometry.

In experiments, DWMP improved obstacle traversal success rates by about 10% over strong existing baselines in simulation. Furthermore, when deployed on a real full-sized Unitree G1 humanoid robot, it demonstrated the ability to stably traverse randomized overhead obstacles and narrow corridors.
contributions: Proposed DWMP (Dual World Model Policy), which separately models low-dimensional, nonlinear proprioception (via Koopman linearization) and high-dimensional, redundant depth vision (via RSSM stochastic compression).

Built a two-stage training scheme that pre-trains the dual world models using diverse exploration trajectories from a privileged teacher policy, then fine-tunes them during the student's online adaptation.
Demonstrated superior generalization in depth reconstruction on unseen obstacle environments as well as a roughly 10% improvement in simulation traversal success rate over baselines.
Achieved successful sim-to-real autonomous traversal on a real full-sized Unitree G1 humanoid robot under randomized obstacle layouts not seen during training.

sections.heading: Why separate proprioception and vision into dual world models?
sections.summary: Traversing humanoid obstacles requires integrating two sensing modalities with completely different physical characteristics: internal motion states and external obstacle geometry. This paper proposes DWMP, combining a Koopman model that linearizes nonlinear proprioceptive dynamics with an RSSM that compresses and predicts depth images.
sections.details:
When a humanoid robot navigates an unknown obstacle course, both proprioceptive observations (joint states and body posture) and egocentric visual observations (looking forward) are indispensable. Recently, teacher-student distillation has become the standard recipe: a "teacher" policy is trained with full privileged environment information in simulation, and an onboard-sensor-only "student" policy is trained to imitate it.

However, most prior work simply concatenates these two streams or pairs raw proprioception with vision compressed via a standard convolutional neural network (CNN). This setup limits the student policy to being a purely reactive motion imitator, because it fails to capture the underlying temporal dynamics—how the robot's body will move next and how the visual scene will shift as a consequence.

The key insight here is that the two modalities have diametrically opposed properties:
- **Proprioception**: Low-dimensional, yet its dynamics are governed by severe nonlinearities from contacts and joint mechanics. Standard policy networks like MLPs struggle to extract predictive control patterns directly from raw signals.
- **Egocentric depth images**: Extremely high-dimensional and susceptible to camera jitter and noise, even though only the geometric layout of obstacles truly matters.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose lifting proprioception into a latent space where temporal evolution is linear via the Koopman operator, while stochastically compressing and predicting visual observations with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM). Pre-training the world models on the teacher's exploration logs and fine-tuning them during student learning yields an approximate 10% boost in simulation success rate and enables successful traversal on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid.

sections.heading: The evolution of world models and legged obstacle traversal
sections.summary: This section reviews Koopman operator methods for dynamics prediction alongside visual world models such as Dreamer. It also clarifies where DWMP stands within vision-guided obstacle avoidance and traversal research for bipedal robots.
sections.details:
Related work can be divided into two main threads: world model applications and humanoid obstacle traversal.

### II-A World Models for Robot Dynamics and Perception
In model-based reinforcement learning, predictive world models play a central role. In dynamical systems, Koopman operator theory has gained traction by mapping nonlinear state transitions into a higher-dimensional space of observable functions where the dynamics behave linearly. Because predictions in a Koopman model boil down to simple matrix multiplications, it is exceptionally well-suited for real-time motion control.
In computer vision and RL, RSSM (Recurrent State-Space Model), popularized by the Dreamer series, has become the standard technique for extracting compact latent sequences from high-dimensional frames. However, conventional visual world models often force proprioception and visual inputs into the exact same latent representation. DWMP distinguishes itself by strictly assigning dedicated roles: linearizing dynamics with Koopman and compressing vision with RSSM.

### II-B Humanoid Robot Obstacle Traversal Policy
For bipedal locomotion under partial observability, distilling from a privileged teacher to a student is the conventional path. Recent advances include encoding the spatial relationship to obstacles as collision-avoidance directions (HumanoidPF) or falling back to blind locomotion when vision drops out (VB-Com). Nevertheless, these methods do not explicitly model the temporal evolution of both the robot's transition dynamics and the visual scene. DWMP fills this gap, drastically improving real-world traversal stability by providing the policy with structured predictive representations.

sections.heading: Designing the dual world model: Koopman meets RSSM
sections.summary: Framed as a POMDP, this section details Auto-Koopman (which maps proprioception into a linear latent space) and DepthDreamer (which stochastically compresses and predicts depth images). It employs a two-stage training scheme combining teacher pre-training with online adaptation to the student's behavior.
sections.details:
The overall architecture and training pipeline are structured as follows:

### III-A Problem Formulation and Input-Output
The task is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP).
- **Observation $\mathbf{o}_t$**: Proprioception $\mathbf{o}_t^{\text{prop}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_p}$—consisting of joint angles $\mathbf{q}_t$, joint velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_t$, gravity vector $\mathbf{g}_t$, base linear and angular velocities $\mathbf{v}_t, \boldsymbol{\omega}_t$, and target relative position $\mathbf{p}_t^{\text{target}}$—alongside egocentric depth image $\mathbf{o}_t^{\text{vis}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}$ from a head camera.
- **Action $\mathbf{a}_t$**: Target positions for lower-body joints, which are converted into motor torques via high-frequency PD controllers.

### III-B Koopman-Based Dynamics World Model
To model nonlinear proprioceptive transitions, an Auto-Koopman network is introduced. An encoder $\phi$ with an Observation Function Transformation Layer (OFTL) at its input lifts the state into a high-dimensional latent space $\mathbf{z}^{\text{prop}}_t = \phi(\mathbf{o}_t^{\text{prop}}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$. In this latent space, state transitions are governed by a linear operator $\mathbf{K}$ such that $\mathbf{z}^{\text{prop}}_{t+1} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{z}^{\text{prop}}_t$. A decoder $\psi$ reconstructs the original observation, and the network is trained by minimizing the sum of reconstruction error and multi-step linear prediction error.

### III-C RSSM-Based Visual World Model (DepthDreamer)
For depth images, DepthDreamer utilizes an RSSM inspired by DreamerV3. It maintains a deterministic recurrent state $\mathbf{z}^{\text{vis}}_t$ (updated via GRU) and a stochastic state $\mathbf{s}_t$ sampled from a VAE encoder. The model optimizes an evidence lower bound (ELBO) combining image reconstruction loss, reward prediction loss, and KL divergence regularization between posterior and prior distributions.

### III-D Policy Input and Co-Training Scheme
Rather than receiving raw sensor signals, the policy network $\pi_\theta$ receives the fused features $\mathbf{x}_t^{\text{policy}} = [\mathbf{z}^{\text{prop}}_t, \mathbf{z}_t^{\text{vis}}]$ extracted by the dual world models. Consequently, the policy issues joint commands based on cleanly organized representations of both immediate body dynamics and upcoming obstacle geometry.

Training proceeds in two stages (Figure F1):
1. **Phase 1 (Pre-training)**: A dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\text{explore}}$ containing rich collision and avoidance trajectories is collected from the privileged teacher's training logs to pre-train the dual world models offline.
2. **Phase 2 (Student Learning & Fine-Tuning)**: Forward transition layers of the pre-trained models are frozen, while the encoders remain trainable to adapt to the student's own action distribution. The encoders are fine-tuned on replay buffer data while simultaneously optimizing task reward maximization and behavioral cloning (BC loss) toward the teacher.

captions.F2: Structure of the Dual World Model. Top: The Auto-Koopman network lifts proprioception into a linear latent space via an OFTL layer and predicts temporal evolution with a linear operator. Bottom: The DepthDreamer network compresses depth images into a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) using CNNs and GRUs, predicting and reconstructing visual observations and rewards for the next frame.

sections.heading: Simulation benchmarks and obstacle traversal on a physical humanoid
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted in the MuJoCo simulator and on a physical Unitree G1 robot. Two-stage learning significantly reduced visual reconstruction errors on unseen terrains and outperformed baselines by about 10% in simulation traversal success. High pass rates were also demonstrated on the real robot under randomized obstacle layouts.
sections.details:
Experiments were performed using the full-sized Unitree G1 humanoid robot in the MuJoCo physics engine and in real-world environments.

### IV-A & IV-B Experimental Setup and Effect of Two-Stage Learning
Obstacles included overhead ceiling beams (Ceil), ground hurdle bars (Bar), narrow pathways (Narrow), and composite layouts such as Mbar and Mceilbar (Figure F3).
Comparing models with and without Phase 1 pre-training revealed that warming up on teacher exploration logs led to immediate, substantially lower validation reconstruction losses during student training, along with a significantly lower final convergence value. Diverse falls and recovery attempts present in the exploration logs provide a solid foundation for robust visual representations.

### IV-C Quality of Visual Representations
Depth image reconstruction errors were evaluated across unseen obstacle terrains (Figure F5). Compared to a standard VAE or a pure CNN baseline lacking temporal dynamics modeling, the proposed DWM exhibited minimal error spikes on unseen terrains. Explicitly modeling robot motion dynamics allows the system to accurately predict how the visual scene transforms as the body moves.

### IV-D Obstacle Traversal Performance in Simulation
As shown in Table I, the proposed method achieved high success rates on complex composite obstacles (such as Mceilbar) compared to conventional teacher-student distillation baselines, yielding an overall success rate improvement of roughly 10%. Furthermore, removing the Koopman model led to severe oscillations in lateral (Y-axis) velocity and position, whereas including the Koopman representation suppressed jitter and produced smooth, stable stepping (Figure F6, Figure F7).

### IV-E Real Humanoid Robot Deployment
DWMP was deployed on the physical Unitree G1 across three test environments: Ceil, Mceilbar, and Narrow. During real-world testing, obstacle placements were randomized and differed from simulation layouts. Compared to a direct distillation baseline from a privileged teacher (HumanoidPF distillation), the proposed method achieved much higher pass rates (Table III), proving that onboard head depth observations are correctly interpreted to avoid collisions.

Evaluated terrains require whole-body coordination, including crouching under overhead obstacles ("ceil"), stepping over hurdles ("bar"), squeezing through narrow gaps ("narrow"), and composite setups like "Mbar" and frame-like "Mceilbar".
captions.F5: Comparison of depth reconstruction error (MSE) across seen and unseen obstacle terrains. Compared to standard VAE- and CNN-based methods, the proposed method (DWM, orange curve) maintains consistently lower error on unseen obstacles and suppresses sharp error spikes when approaching obstacles.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future directions
sections.summary: By unifying Koopman linearization for proprioception and RSSM compression for vision, DWMP enables robust humanoid obstacle traversal. Future work aims to expand to dynamic obstacles and integrate tighter long-term trajectory planning.
sections.details:
This work presented DWMP (Dual World Model Policy), enabling humanoid robots to autonomously navigate cluttered obstacle terrains using onboard sensing alone.

The core of this approach lies in tailoring dedicated model structures to two fundamentally different modalities: Koopman operators for highly nonlinear proprioception, and an RSSM for high-dimensional visual geometry. In addition, an efficient pipeline repurposes rich exploration trajectories from teacher training for world model pre-training, followed by fine-tuning during student learning.

Improvements in simulation traversal success and zero-shot obstacle traversal on the physical Unitree G1 strongly validate the effectiveness of multimodal world models for humanoid whole-body control. Looking ahead, the authors highlight adapting to dynamic scenes with moving humans or obstacles, as well as integrating long-horizon motion planning leveraging the world model's internal imagination capabilities.

takeaways: Rather than naively concatenating multimodal inputs, tailoring representation models to their distinct physical properties (nonlinear dynamics for proprioception vs. high-dimensional spatial redundancy for vision) is remarkably effective.

Even for highly nonlinear robotic locomotion, lifting states into a latent space via Koopman operators turns complex transitions into linear predictive features that are easy for policy networks to exploit.
Exploration logs from teacher policies in RL distillation should not be discarded; reusing them as a pre-training dataset for world models significantly boosts the quality of initial representations.

Equipping visual representations with dynamics prediction (RSSM) allows the robot to anticipate camera shifts caused by its own movement, enhancing sim-to-real robustness against unseen obstacle layouts.
limitations: All obstacles evaluated in this study are static; performance in dynamic environments featuring moving humans or other robots remains unverified.

The predictive capabilities of the world models are used strictly for feature conditioning and encoder fine-tuning, stopping short of full latent-space long-horizon trajectory planning—a signature capability of Dreamer.
How broadly the linear evolution matrix of the Koopman model can generalize across extreme whole-body agility (such as jumping or fall recovery) without breakdown warrants deeper investigation.
